marks.label: Calmer
marks.ask: When should I use belly breathing?

faq.a: Belly breathing means breathing slowly and deeply so your tummy rises and falls. A dome-shaped muscle under your lungs, called the diaphragm, does the work.
asks: How do I do belly breathing?

faq.q: How does slow breathing calm my heart?
faq.a: Your heart naturally slows a little each time you breathe out. Long, slow breaths out send a calm message to your body, so your heart rate drops and your muscles relax.
asks: Why does deep breathing calm me down?

faq.q: Why should I breathe in through my nose?
faq.a: Your nose warms and cleans the air, and breathing through it helps you breathe more slowly. If your nose is blocked, breathing gently through your mouth is fine.
asks: Is it better to breathe through your nose?

faq.q: When should I use belly breathing?
faq.a: Any time you feel angry, worried, scared or cannot sleep. It also helps before a test, a race or a performance. Practise when you are calm so it is easy later.

faq.q: What if breathing slowly makes me dizzy?
faq.a: Breathe gently, not hugely; the aim is slower, not bigger. If you feel dizzy, go back to normal breathing and tell a grown-up if it keeps happening.
asks: Why do I feel dizzy when I take deep breaths?

facts: The diaphragm, a dome-shaped muscle under your lungs, does most of the work when you breathe in.
Your heart naturally speeds up a little when you breathe in and slows down a little when you breathe out.

wrong.1: Squeezing your tummy in is the opposite of belly breathing.
